source: Kuittinen & Sajaniemi (2003) First results of an experiment on using roles of variables in teaching, PPIG 15
finding: Sajaniemi's roles of variables: a role is a stereotypic way a variable is used in a program. Roles capture tacit expert knowledge in a form novices can be taught.
numbers: Ten roles are said to cover 99% of variables in novice-level programs; one count in the paper gives 84% coverage for a smaller role set.
limits: Coverage figures come from the authors' own program corpus.
agent_relevance: Background: a small named vocabulary of variable uses is a cheap shared notation. Our schema could name a few recurring state roles.

source: Kuittinen & Sajaniemi (2003) First results of an experiment on using roles of variables in teaching, PPIG 15
finding: Design: three groups in a five-week Pascal course. Traditional (no roles), roles throughout, roles plus the PlanAni role-based animator in exercises. Same lectures, programs and exercise tasks except for role teaching.
numbers: 80 students randomly split into three groups, 11 more enrolled later, 60 sat the exam, 44 kept after dropping those who attended under 40% of lectures or exercises.
limits: Attrition cut 80 to 44. First-semester CS undergraduates, one course, one site.
agent_relevance: Small analysed N is a warning for any education study we cite.

source: Kuittinen & Sajaniemi (2003) First results of an experiment on using roles of variables in teaching, PPIG 15
finding: Exam results: no significant group difference on program simulation, program construction or the non-variable questions. Only roles vs animation differed, on program comprehension.
numbers: Comprehension: roles group best, animation group worst, roles vs animation significant (two-tailed). Fully correct comprehension answers averaged grade 4.6 traditional, 5.0 roles, 4.1 animation. Construction: roles and animation groups above traditional, not significant.
limits: The 2003 paper claims trends only. Graders favoured detailed statement-by-statement answers over high-level ones, which may have penalised the animation group.
agent_relevance: 'Roles help' is weak evidence: trends, not clean effects.

source: Kuittinen & Sajaniemi (2003) First results of an experiment on using roles of variables in teaching, PPIG 15
finding: Students used role names unprompted in exam answers; almost no role was misassigned.
numbers: 35% of the roles group and 35% of the animation group used role names; 0% of the traditional group. Two subjects in the roles group made role errors.
limits: Shows vocabulary uptake, not better performance.
agent_relevance: A model given role labels may reuse them; whether that helps is untested here.

source: Kuittinen & Sajaniemi (2003) First results of an experiment on using roles of variables in teaching, PPIG 15
finding: Animation group described programs at the data level (what each variable does over time). Traditional and roles groups described them at the operation level. Data-level summaries match Pennington's sign of deeper comprehension.
numbers: Qualitative classification of exam answers; no counts beyond the 44 analysed.
limits: Exercise software differed: PlanAni users watched variables, debugger users followed code.
agent_relevance: Good comprehenders think in data flow; asking a model to restate code as variable roles might mimic that.

source: Kuittinen & Sajaniemi (2004) Teaching roles of variables in elementary programming courses, ITiCSE
finding: Abstract page only: gives teaching techniques for roles from learning theory; results suggest roles let students process programs like good code comprehenders and animation helps adoption.
numbers: No numbers on the abstract page.
limits: Only the abstract was read.
agent_relevance: Same limits as the 2003 data.

source: Sajaniemi & Kuittinen (2005) An experiment on using roles of variables in teaching introductory programming, Computer Science Education 15(1):59-82
finding: Journal report of the same three-group Pascal experiment. Authors conclude students understand and apply roles and gain a framework for mentally processing programs; the animator fosters adoption.
numbers: Abstract only: ten roles cover 99% of variables in novice programs; three groups.
limits: Abstract only; full text not read.
agent_relevance: Candidate for the most rigorous version of the finding.

source: Nikula, Sajaniemi, Tedre & Wray (2007) Python and roles of variables in introductory programming, JITE 6:199-214
finding: Field report from three institutions adopting Python and roles. Authors report students wrote working code early, found it easy and interesting, passed with good grades, and drop-out was low.
numbers: Summary page gives no sample sizes or effect sizes.
limits: Uncontrolled before-after report; Python and roles are confounded; no comparison group.
agent_relevance: Existence claim only.

source: Sajaniemi (2008) Psychology of programming: looking into programmers' heads, Human Technology 4(1)
finding: Overview cited by Wikipedia as a field reference. Could not be opened: the journal site redirected and later fetches were blocked.
numbers: none
limits: Not read. Do not cite its content.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Weinberg (1971, Silver ed. 1998) The Psychology of Computer Programming
finding: Founding book on programmers as people and teams. The book was not read; Wikipedia lists it as a reference.
numbers: none verified
limits: Not read. No numbers cited.
agent_relevance: Egoless review culture parallels our rule that the model must not grade its own text.

source: Wikipedia: Psychology of programming (summary fetch)
finding: The page has no language-design or education section. It says research began in the late 1970s and early 1980s, that Shneiderman listed research destinations (refine languages, special-purpose languages, better tools) at the first Empirical Studies of Programmers workshop, and that the ESP and PPIG workshop series followed.
numbers: none
limits: Secondary source, read through a summarising fetch.
agent_relevance: Confirms this subfield is thin background for us.

source: Shneiderman (1980) Software Psychology: Human Factors in Computer and Information Systems
finding: Founding book applying experimental psychology to language features and tools. Not opened.
numbers: none verified
limits: Not read. Avoid quoting results.
agent_relevance: Founding case for testing language and tool features with users instead of opinion.

source: Pritchard (2015) Frequency distribution of error messages, PLATEAU
finding: Counted which error messages novices meet. In both Python and Java data, after grouping identical messages, frequencies resemble a Zipf-Mandelbrot distribution: a few messages account for most events.
numbers: Python (CS Circles): 640000 runs ended in an error; 283 distinct messages, 17 occurred twice and 42 once. Java (BlueJ Blackbox): about 5 million events; 572 distinct messages, 65 twice and 127 once. Top Java error: cannot find symbol.
limits: Two datasets, one per language; Java reports at compile time what Python reports at run time.
agent_relevance: A handful of error types dominate, so a short library of error explanations covers most debug cases.

source: Leinonen et al. (2023) Using large language models to enhance programming error messages
finding: Codex explained Python error messages and suggested fixes. Explanations were mostly understandable; fixes were often wrong.
numbers: Explanations comprehensible in 67% to 100% of cases by message. Fix correct only 33% of the time (17% to 56% by message). Judged an improvement over the original message in 54% of cases (22% for 'unexpected EOF while parsing', 78% for 'can't assign to function call'). 9 error messages x 3 programs x 3 temperatures.
limits: Small hand-judged set, one 2022 model; later models score higher.
agent_relevance: Trust the explanation, verify the fix by running tests.

source: Denny, Kumar & Giacaman (2023) Conversing with Copilot: prompt engineering for CS1
finding: Copilot on 166 public CS1 problems: about half solved first try; rewording the problem in plain language solved most of the rest.
numbers: 47.6% solved on first attempt; 60.9% of the remaining problems solved after prompt rewording. Largest failure categories: Conceptual and Verbose prompts.
limits: One tool version; public problems may be in training data; the authors did the rewording.
agent_relevance: Task wording matters. Supports restating a problem before solving.

source: Babe et al. (2023) StudentEval: a benchmark of student-written prompts for code LLMs
finding: 80 beginners wrote 1,749 prompts for 48 problems. Student prompts often failed on problems that expert descriptions solve easily. Sampling noise made some prompts look better or worse than they were.
numbers: Mean pass@1 from function signatures alone 0.0519 (Codex). Best models about 63-65% on first-success prompts, about 51% on last-success, about 7-9% on first-failure, versus about 30% on HumanEval for the same models. 200 samples per prompt. Nearly 10% of successful prompts unreliable for small models, under 3% for large.
limits: One course family, Python only, 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Prompt quality drives results. Judge a prompt over repeated samples, not one run.

source: Kazemitabaar et al. (2023) Studying the effect of AI code generators on supporting novice learners, CHI
finding: Controlled study of 69 analysed novices (33 Codex, 36 baseline), 10 sessions. With Codex they did better while using it, and not worse without it.
numbers: Training authoring tasks: 1.15x completion, 0.59x errors, 1.8x correctness, about 0.57x time. Syntax errors per task 0.87 vs 1.67 (t(67)=3.65, p=.001, d=0.88). Errors per task 1.28 vs 2.17 (p=.004, d=0.74). Pre-test 62.7% vs 60% (p=.67).
limits: Ages 10-17, N fell from 90 to 69, one course, Scratch then Python.
agent_relevance: Tools remove syntax errors fast; they do not show that understanding improved.

source: Kazemitabaar et al. (2023) Studying the effect of AI code generators on supporting novice learners, CHI
finding: One-week retention test: Codex group nominally better but not significant; more errors when writing with no starter code. Benefit concentrated in high prior-score learners.
numbers: Retention authoring 59.1% vs 49.8% (p=.262, d=0.28); modifying 47.5% vs 34.8% (p=.092, d=0.41); authoring errors 1.58 vs 0.99 (t(67)=2.08, p=.042, d=0.51). Codex group used documentation far less.
limits: Subgroup split by pre-test is post hoc; low-prior learners showed little retention benefit.
agent_relevance: Offloading syntax may leave reasoning and lookup habits weaker.

source: Kazemitabaar et al. (2023) How novices use LLM-based code generators to solve CS1 coding tasks in a self-paced environment, Koli Calling
finding: Thematic analysis of 33 learners aged 10-17 over 45 tasks. Four coding approaches: AI Single Prompt, AI Step-by-Step, Hybrid, Manual. Single Prompt gave the best authoring scores but the lowest scores on later code modification; learners who switched between manual and AI coding had higher learning outcomes.
numbers: AI Single Prompt used on 630 tasks, authoring M=96% (SD 16). Step-by-Step 82 tasks, Hybrid 252, Manual 397. Table extraction is interleaved, so other cells (authoring 63-77%, modifying 55-73%) cannot be mapped to rows with confidence. 66% of prompts pasted the whole task description (n=503); 92% of start-of-task prompts followed no attempt.
limits: Observational; approach is self-selected.
agent_relevance: One-shot generation maximises output but loses learning. Decompose then check keeps the user engaged.

source: Savelka et al. (2023) Large language models (GPT) struggle to answer multiple-choice questions about code
finding: 530 MCQs from three Python courses. GPT models did much worse on questions containing code than on text-only ones; output-tracing and true/false-about-code were hardest.
numbers: text-davinci-003: text-only 134/172 = 77.9%; with code 53/110 = 48.2%. text-davinci-002 with code 52.7%. Jaccard baseline with code 20.0%.
limits: Early 2023 GPT-3 models; later models are far stronger. Table text is jumbled in extraction.
agent_relevance: Tracing code by reading is a weak spot; running the code is more reliable than asking the model to predict output.

source: Sarsa, Denny, Hellas & Leinonen (2022) Automatic generation of programming exercises and code explanations with large language models, ICER
finding: Codex generated CS1 exercises and code explanations. Most were sensible and novel, but many exercises failed their own tests.
numbers: 120 exercises: 75.0% sensible, 81.8% novel, 76.7% sample solution matched. Programmatic: 84.6% had a sample solution, 89.7% of those ran, 70.8% had tests, only 30.9% of test sets passed (51 of 165). Mean coverage 98%. Explanations covered about 90% of code; 67.2% of explanation lines correct.
limits: One 2022 model, judged by four researchers.
agent_relevance: Generated solutions and generated tests disagree often; cross-check by executing.

source: Denny et al. (2023) Promptly: using prompt problems to teach learners how to effectively use AI code generators
finding: Proposes the Prompt Problem: the student writes a natural-language prompt, an LLM produces code, hidden tests judge it. A pilot with 36 graduate students showed many prompts were unclear or the task was misunderstood.
numbers: Pilot N=36; results qualitative.
limits: Concept paper with a pilot; no controlled learning outcome in the part read.
agent_relevance: Frames specification-writing as the skill, matching our restate-and-test view.

source: Liang, Yang & Myers (2024) A large-scale survey on the usability of AI programming assistants, ICSE
finding: Survey of 410 developers. Uses: fewer keystrokes, speed, recalling syntax. Barriers: output misses functional or non-functional needs, and the tool is hard to control.
numbers: Motivation: reduce keystrokes 86%, faster 76%, recall syntax 68%, starting points 50%, brainstorm 36%. Barriers: requirements not met 54%, hard to control 48%. Cited telemetry: Copilot acceptance 23.3% TypeScript, 27.9% JavaScript, 28.8% Python.
limits: Self-report, volunteer sample, 2022-23 tools.
agent_relevance: Control over output matters; a program-driven loop gives control.

source: Barke, James & Polikarpova (2023) Grounded Copilot: how programmers interact with code-generating models, OOPSLA
finding: Grounded theory from 20 participants across four languages: use is bimodal. Acceleration mode: knows the next step, uses the tool for speed. Exploration mode: unsure, uses the tool to explore options.
numbers: N=20; four languages; qualitative.
limits: Small sample, Copilot only, no outcome effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Two modes suggest two prompts: execute a known plan versus propose options.

source: Prather et al. (2024) The widening gap: benefits and harms of generative AI for novice programmers, ICER
finding: Replication with GenAI added, using observation, interview and eye tracking. Some students accelerated; those who struggled kept their metacognitive problems, which AI made worse, and ended with an illusion of competence.
numbers: 21 lab sessions (27 enrolled, 21 opted in); 20 of 21 completed.
limits: Small single-institution sample, qualitative coding.
agent_relevance: AI help can widen gaps. Our agent needs an external check, not belief in its own progress.

source: Liffiton et al. (2023) CodeHelp: using LLMs with guardrails for scalable support in programming classes
finding: Tool gives hints but withholds full solutions; each query is one-shot; instructors set guardrails. Students used it steadily across a semester.
numbers: Survey 45 of 52 students. About half the class used it each week; about 70% in four or more weeks; roughly 80% submitted 10+ queries, about 50% 30+; 7 of 49 submitted over 100, one over 600.
limits: One course; self-report; no learning-outcome comparison.
agent_relevance: Output-form guardrails are cheap and accepted, matching a guide-not-answer rule.

source: Pea (1986) language-independent conceptual bugs; Stefik & Siebert (2013) syntax experiments; Hanenberg (2010) static typing experiment
finding: Not opened: ACM returned 403 and the search budget was gone. Listed only as standard citations to chase in a later pass.
numbers: none verified
limits: Do not quote results from memory.
agent_relevance: Follow up later.
